Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.explanation: The profile omits both Triggers and Threat entirely, yet includes carrying a weapon and persistent on-guard appraisals. For a 60-year-old male with military trauma, these items are individually plausible, but together they imply an active current-danger/threat system that is not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes and sits poorly with the formulation, where Threat and Triggers are not linked to the active network.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: 'I have to be on guard all the time' functions more like a live threat appraisal, but the formulation centers the case on a Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Threat inactive. In the absence of any other threat-focused items, this item is the main source of incoherence.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: 'Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning' implies salient cue-driven triggering, but all Triggers edges are inactive and no Trigger items are selected. That does not by itself make triggered recall impossible, but combined with the otherwise appraisal/guilt/identity-focused formulation and profile, it is the least coherent memory item.

issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: This item is difficult to reconcile with the formulation because Threat is not otherwise represented in the self-report and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The rest of the profile is organized around guilt/identity loss and trauma memory, whereas constant threat scanning implies an active current-threat focus that is not supported by the selected Threat, Trigger, Appraisal, or Memory items. The avoidance items fit the military trauma context, but this hypervigilant checking behavior appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

vignette: John is a 60-year-old European-American male who has served in the military and currently works at a warehouse. Over the past few months, he has increasingly isolated himself from his loved ones and struggles with intense emotional distress when recalling his traumatic experiences during service. His wife notices that John avoids certain locations and activities that remind him of his time in the military. John vividly recalls a specific incident where he was part of a mission that resulted in significant loss of life among his fellow soldiers. He had come to believe that he survived only because others did not, which has led to intense feelings of guilt. When he thinks about this event, it feels as though he is reliving the terror and fear all over again. John often cannot find words to describe what happened, leaving him feeling trapped in a silent loop of memory. John's sense that the world is inherently dangerous exacerbates his maladaptive strategies. For instance, he avoids wearing clothes similar to those he wore during his deployment because they serve as potent reminders of the traumatic event. This avoidance behavior has extended to other areas of his life; he no longer visits places where he might encounter people or environments reminiscent of his military service. The guilt and loss of identity John feels have further deepened his maladaptive strategies. He avoids thinking about the incident altogether, often turning to distractions like alcohol or work at the warehouse, which temporarily alleviate his distress but do not address the underlying issues. These avoidance behaviors, in turn, reinforce his negative appraisals. For example, every time he encounters something that reminds him of the event-such as a particular uniform or a certain location-he is reminded of his survival guilt and how the world remains a dangerous place. John's wife has noticed these changes in his behavior and emotional state but finds it difficult to understand why he seems so distant and preoccupied. Recently, John had an incident at work where he became highly agitated when a colleague inadvertently mentioned something related to military operations. This led him to realize that his current coping mechanisms were no longer sustainable and that the cycle of avoidance was only worsening his condition. John's most pressing fear is that he will never fully recover from these traumatic memories and will continue to feel disconnected from himself and others. He hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to process his experiences without being overwhelmed by guilt and terror, allowing him to regain a sense of self and reconnect with the world around him.
